parts.problem_md:
A group of students have investigated the physical processes involved in an extreme weather event, by recording a weather diary.

(i) Identify one risk that the students may identify when undertaking a risk assessment for this investigation.

(1)

(ii) State one way that this risk could be managed.

(1)
parts.solution_md:
(i) Award 1 mark for any reasonable risk in the context of this environment:

- ( Fallingover in ) strong winds ** (1)**.
- Exposure sun burn ** (1)**
- Slips / trips/ bumps ** (1)**
- An extreme weather event ** (1)**
- Heavy rain / flooding ** (1)**
- Falling masonry / building collapse ** (1)**

Accept any other appropriate response.   
**Reject inaccurate measurements as not part of risk assessment.  Also reject earthquake risks. **

(ii) Award 1 mark for any reasonable risk in the context of what was identified in (5ai):

- Avoid exposed locations / out in the open ** (1)**
- Collecting data once the storm has died down ** (1)**
- Use secondary data ** (1)**
- Checking local requirements plans etc ** (1)**
- Waking with care ** (1)**
- Working in groups ** (1)**
- Wearing sunscreen suntan lotion ** (1)**
- Staying away from a storm ** (1)**
- Using a weather forecast ** (1)**
- Remote collection of weather data ** (1)**

Accept any other appropriate response.   
**Reject approaches that do not match (5ai). Reject to stay indoors as weather data cannot be collected indoors. **

parts.solution_md:

parts.problem_md:
A group of students has undertaken an enquiry that investigated changes in the weather as part of their studies into hazardous environments.

Explain **one** factor that affected the students' choice of data collection sites.
parts.solution_md:
They could have chosen sites that represented the study area's urban-to-rural gradient. **[1]** Each site is a fixed distance from the city centre to measure and compare air temperature changes with distance. **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a** point-marked** approach.
> 
> - **One mark** for identifying a valid factor
> - **One mark** for how that factor influenced site selection
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Alternative information that could be provided in the answer includes:
> 
> - Accessibility and safety: sites needed to be reachable on foot or by public transport and had to be in publicly accessible locations such as parks or pavements
> - Land use type: sites were deliberately chosen in areas of different land use, such as a park, a shopping street and a residential area, to investigate how surface cover affects local temperature
> - Proximity to a fixed reference point: all sites were measured at a known distance from the town hall so that the transect could be accurately reproduced on a follow-up visit
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Describing data collection methods rather than site selection decisions
> - Writing about risk management rather than site choice decisions

> **[exam-tip]**
> The question asks about **site choice,** not what happened on arrival.
> 
> **Think **about how you would choose a particular spot on the beach and not somewhere else.
> 
> **Your **second sentence should begin with 'because' or 'so that' to earn the development mark.

parts.problem_md:
A group of students has undertaken an enquiry that investigated changes in the weather as part of their studies into hazardous environments.

Identify **one **health and safety risk that the students could face during their enquiry. Explain the impact this risk could have had.
parts.solution_md:
One risk is heat exhaustion caused by working outdoors during a heatwave. **[1] **If a student became severely overheated while collecting data, they could have collapsed or lost consciousness, requiring emergency medical assistance. **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command words '**identify**' and '**explain**' together mean you must name the risk and then state what harm it could cause. Do not describe how the risk was managed.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a** point-marked** approach.
> 
> - **One mark** for identifying a relevant health and safety risk
> - **One mark** for explaining the impact of that risk, not the management of it
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Alternative information that could be provided in the answer includes:
> 
> - Dehydration caused by working in extreme heat
> - Traffic hazard when crossing roads or recording data on busy urban streets
> - Sunburn from prolonged exposure to direct sunlight
> - Tripping on uneven pavements or kerbs while moving between sites
> - Any other appropriate response

> **[exam-tip]**
> **A risk** is something that could go wrong. **Management **is how you tried to prevent it.
> 
> **This** question only wants the risk and its impact. Imagine the worst realistic outcome and describe it clearly.
> 
> **Do not **describe how you stayed safe.

parts.problem_md: Outline three factors that should be considered when choosing a suitable sampling site for a microclimate investigation.
parts.solution_md:
Credit any valid factor stated with 1 mark. Must include at least two meteorological consideration for max marks

e.g. different surroundings ** (1)**. 2nd mark for this to be exemplified twice e.g. south-facing aspect ** (1)**; sheltered spot ** (1)**; open space ** (1)** …

Allow 1 mark for valid access or health & safety consideration e.g. trespass** (1)**; traffic ** (1)**….

Each valid factor carries a 2nd mark for description re suitability e.g.

- open space ** (1)** > gives more “natural” reading for area** (1)**
- trespass ** (1)** > ensure permission acquired ** (1)** Do not credit two separate points in one section.

parts.problem_md:
Outline each of the three following sampling methods used in geographical investigations.

- random sampling
- stratified sampling
- systematic sampling
parts.solution_md:
Accept for up to max marks answers defining each ofthe three methods.

Systematic sampling = sample taken in regular way (1)e.g. every tenth person; every 100 metres ** (1)**...

Random sampling = sample taken based on equalchance of inclusion for all (1) e.g. using randomnumbers table; drawn from a hat** (1)**….

Stratified sampling = samples are selected according to a known characteristic ** (1)** e.g. age-distribution ofpopulation in an opinions survey; sites reflecting rocktype in vegetation survey ** (1)**….

For responses focussing directly on differences mark on a similar points basis.
